papers.title: Conceptualizing the process of experiential acceptance during an episode of anxiety: A qualitative study of individuals with prior experience in mindfulness- and acceptance-based interventions.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Experiential acceptance refers to the capacity to be open to internal experiences without attempting to change or avoid them. Although acceptance is a core emotion regulation strategy within mindfulness- and acceptance-based interventions (MABIs) and a protective factor for mental health, its conceptualization and implementation remain unclear and ambiguous. The aim of this study was to clarify and develop a model of accepting anxiety as experienced by individuals with prior experience in MABIs. METHOD: Twenty-six participants from a non-clinical sample with varying levels of prior experience in MABIs took part in semi-structured interviews exploring their experience of accepting anxiety. Data collection and analysis followed the principles of Grounded Theory to generate a data-driven model of the acceptance process. RESULTS: We identified a five-stage dynamic model involving distinct processes: observing through the body with attentional focus on interoceptive experience; identifying and acknowledging anxiety; validating and normalizing the experience through validation and self-compassion; observing from an observer stance characterized by decentering; and maintaining flexible contact with the experience via interoceptive exposure and nonreactivity. We also identified facilitating factors that support engagement in the acceptance process. CONCLUSION: These findings refine the understanding of acceptance as a multidimensional emotion regulation process by highlighting an active dynamic involving multiple mechanisms underlying the acceptance of anxiety. As experienced by individuals with prior MABI experience, this model provides a framework for developing more targeted clinical interventions and for investigating individual and contextual variability in these subprocesses.

papers.title: Affection and Self-Constitution of Consciousness: The Condition of Possibility of Lived Experience in the Phenomenology of Edmund Husserl.
papers.abstract: This article revisits the apparent circularity between temporal self-constitution and affection in Husserl's genetic phenomenology. Rather than treating formal and genetic priority as an exhaustive solution, it proposes a constrained account of constitutive articulation. Temporal self-manifestation specifies a necessary condition for an occurrence to count as lived; associative differentiation provides pre-egoic organization; embodied affective gradients modulate salience; and attentional uptake can sediment new dispositions. These moments are distinguishable by explanatory role but not separable as independently existing stages. The article offers phenomenological criteria for degrees of affection and a non-vicious-circularity test, while confronting Michel Henry's account of auto-affection, Didier Franck's analyses of body and time, the phenomenological unconscious, and reports of diminished time-awareness in contemplative experience. The result is a qualified, rather than absolute, thesis: temporal articulation is necessary for identifiable lived succession, but it is not demonstrated to be a condition of every conceivable phenomenal feeling.

papers.title: Psychedelic ego-dissolution: a philosophical and qualitative critique.
papers.abstract: Ego-dissolution is a phenomenon of central interest across interdisciplinary research on psychedelics. In this paper, we present a philosophical and qualitative critique of the claim that ego-dissolution can result in conscious states with no phenomenal sense of self, i.e., states that completely lack any form of self-consciousness. We first turn to recent publications by Chris Letheby and Raphaël Millière, for whom trip reports of experiences induced by 5-MeO-DMT (5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine) present clear evidence for the existence of totally selfless experiential states. Their claim is undermined, we argue, by the fact that they operate with overinflated notions of 'self' and 'self-consciousness,' meaning that more minimal forms are available and arguably still present in 5-MeO-DMT experiences. We then perform a qualitative thematic analysis of 411 5-MeO-DMT trip reports. Pointing to the ambiguous language of the trip reports, the self-admitted inadequacy of the descriptions and the affective dimension of the reported experiences, we argue that claims concerning total selflessness are unwarranted and instead offer an alternative interpretation: extreme ego-dissolution during 5-MeO-DMT experiences involves a radically minimal form of self-consciousness, one in which the identity of the subject is experienced as unfamiliar and underdetermined. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.
